title: vLLM Day-0 Support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview: Plugin Deployment and E2E Inference Acceleration
summary: vLLM supports Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview on day 0 through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin on the released vllm==0.32.0 wheel, with structure-aware kernel fusion, FlashIndexer, W4A8 QAT and DSpark speculative decoding.
story_key: model:vllm|ver:5.5|variant:flash,preview|title:vllm day 0 support for ernie 5 5 flash preview plugin deployment and e2e inferen
content_excerpt: The Baidu ERNIE team has worked with vLLM to bring day-0 support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview to vLLM. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview is a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 280B total parameters and 14B activated per token. It supports a 1M-token context, thinks before it answers, and uses tool calling to carry out long-horizon Agent tasks. vLLM supports the model on release day through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin, a standalone package that you install into the same environment as the official vllm==0.32.0 wheel. Install the released vLLM wheel and the plugin into the same environment. vLLM discovers the plugin automatically through its vllm.general_plugins entrypoint, so there is nothing to import or configure. The following command serves the default FP4 weights on a single 4-GPU node, with DSpark speculative decoding drafting 7 tokens per step: To turn off thinking for a request, pass "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} . Launch commands for 1M context, attention TP and PD disaggregation are in the vLLM-ERNIE README and the vLLM recipe . ERNIE 5.5 Flash was designed with inference cost as a primary goal from the start, weighing activated compute, KV cache size and long-context overhead together. Every component, from the attention structure and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head, was redesigned around that goal. For design and training details, see the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview blog . ERNIE 5.5 Flash introduces several new structures in attention and MoE: low-rank cross-head post-mixing (VHA post-mix), Multi-Router Latent MoE, the MultiMax output head and sigmoid output gating. When implemented op by op from their mathematical definitions, these structures produce many intermediate tensors and pay for them in memory traffic and kernel launches. For each structure, we designed a dedicated fused kernel around its compute and memory-access profile, and folded everything that can be precomputed into the weights at load time. The fused kernels run 1.55× to 6.53× faster than naive implementations. Together, these fusions cover the full forward pass of ERNIE 5.5 Flash, from attention and MoE routing to the output head. They cut the number of kernel launches and the round trips of intermediate tensors through GPU memory while keeping the numerics aligned, and they underpin the model's high inference performance. The Baidu ERNIE inference team developed FlashIndexer, a lightweight indexer acceleration built on dynamic head routing

title: Composing Independently Distilled Memory and Retrieval Policies for Long-Term Agents
summary: Long-lived Web assistants require effective memory and retrieval mechanisms to access information from past user interactions. While these capabilities can be learned through specialized policies, it remains unclear whether specialists trained independently in different environments can be effectively composed without joint optimization. This paper investigates compositional transfer through policy distillation. Memory-writing and sequential retrieval policies are independently distilled from frontier-model action trajectories into 3B models and combined with a fixed answer generator without downstream training. On a LongMemEval-based benchmark, the distilled composition achieves 73.1% accuracy, compared with 36.2% for a composition of existing RL-trained specialists, and also outperforms the evaluated RL-trained compositions on PersonaMem-v2. Component ablations reveal that improvements in individual policies depend on their composition, highlighting the importance of cross-specialist compatibility. Further task-specific adaptation improves accuracy to 75.2% on LongMemEval through RL and 48.9% on PersonaMem-v2 through supervised distillation. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of independent specialist distillation for modular multi-agent systems. Source code and datasets of teacher-generated memory-editing and retrieval trajectories are released to facilitate reproducibility and further research.

title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware
summary: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.

title: GameDojo: Benchmarking Real-Time Interactive Agents in Video Games
summary: Interactive intelligence requires agents to act on observations and adapt to the consequences of actions. Studying these abilities calls for diverse, challenging tasks under controlled conditions. We introduce GameDojo, a controllable interactive gameplay benchmark of 120 boss encounters across 20 games for evaluating model capabilities, learning algorithms, and agent harnesses. Coding agents reconstruct the environments and write gameplay scripts, producing GameDojo-Data with 600 hours of gameplay trajectories. Experiments reveal substantial challenges for frontier models, especially in real-time interaction. Training on GameDojo-Data brings GameDojo-4B to frontier performance, with the strongest real-time performance. We also find joint training improves individual tasks, and learned policies transfer across bosses. Together, these findings establish GameDojo as a challenging and valuable interactive gameplay benchmark for the community. Our project page is at https://gamedojo-benchmark.github.io/ , and our code is at https://github.com/THUSI-Lab/GameDojo .

title: Skip the DRAM Tier: MoRI UMBP Runs the Agentic KV Cache on NVMe
summary: On AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, a MoRI UMBP KV pool on NVMe matched a DRAM pool of the same size within 1% for Kimi-K3 on vLLM, and drives that hold a day of agent KV cost less than DRAM that holds 31 minutes.
story_key: story|title:skip the dram tier mori umbp runs the agentic kv cache on nvme
content_excerpt: Most of the traffic in agentic serving is multi-turn sessions that resend long prefixes. In the AgentX benchmark replaying real Claude Code sessions, the median turn is 142K input tokens, and over 96% of those tokens are a prefix the server has already seen [3] . A KV cache hit means the prefill node only has to process the small delta. A miss forces a full recomputation of the prefix, which burns GPU time and delays the first token. In our 42 runs of Kimi-K3 on vLLM, raising the KV cache hit rate by 1% of prompt tokens, for example from 95% to 96%, was worth about 10% more throughput (Figure 3). A KV cache hit needs the session’s prefix to still be in memory when its next turn arrives. With dozens of sessions open at once, memory runs out. GPU memory goes first, and host DRAM is the usual next tier. But DRAM fills too: Kimi-K3 wrote 2.3 to 4.6 TB of KV to the pool an hour in our runs, so a 1.8 TB DRAM pool, which lists at about $76,000, holds only the last 23 to 47 minutes of it. That led us to a simple question: why not skip the DRAM tier and put vLLM’s KV pool straight on NVMe? We tried it on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs with UMBP, the KV cache pool in AMD’s open-source MoRI library. At the same size, NVMe matched DRAM’s throughput within 1% on Kimi-K3, in two sets of runs on different machines (Figure 1). On a second workload with longer prompts, NVMe came within 1% of a DRAM pool of the same size. The NVMe pool has no DRAM tier: DRAM only buffers new KV on its way to the drives and stages reads, about 80 GB against the DRAM pool’s 1.8 TB. And NVMe’s cost follows the KV it writes, not the KV it holds, so drives rated for Kimi-K3’s writes cost less than that DRAM pool and hold a full day of KV. “Agentic workloads keep sessions open for minutes or hours, and their KV cache quickly outgrows GPU memory and host DRAM. Results like these, with NVMe keeping up with DRAM at the same pool size, change how we think about sizing KV cache capacity in AI clusters. We’re glad to see this work done in the open, in vLLM and MoRI.” — Dennis Kennetz, Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure DeepSeek already keeps agent KV caches on SSD: the deployment notes for its DeepInfer engine describe three days of retention for agent traffic, on about 14.4 TB of SSD per GPU [4] . This work references DeepInfer for the idea of keeping the KV cache on SSD and for two of its techniques, layer-wise loading and bounded replay, which we test on vLLM below. Figure 1.

title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
summary: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo, an open-source runtime for Linux. It helps teams protect running systems while they roll out patches.
story_key: story|title:openai and cisco introduce shirudo
content_excerpt: An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart. We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day. Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline. Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running. Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems. Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it. Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed. Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. title: Lessons from 12 Evals: Where They Break and What to Measure Instead
summary: How benchmarks are built, the bugs they have, and hot takes on what should change.
story_key: story|title:lessons from 12 evals where they break and what to measure instead
content_excerpt: As models ship faster, eval scores are often the first thing we learn about a new model. But how much weight should we put in them? In eight of twelve public evals studied, there’s evidence the grader failed work that should have passed. And even when the grader gets it right, many benchmarks measure what’s easy rather than what matters, and should instead focus on reliability, work velocity, multi-turn collaboration, etc. Here, we’ll cover the common patterns and principles, the errors models make, and where current benchmarks fall short. I’ll also share what we’re getting wrong and what should change, including why average pass rate isn’t enough and why dollars are the wrong measure of cost. Finally, we’ll walk through twelve evals: four on coding and science, six on knowledge work, and two on browsing and computer use. By the end, you’ll know what to trust in a benchmark and what to question. In addition, eval benchmarks are increasingly maintained like software. They ship versioned releases and accept fixes through issues and pull requests. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 retired 30 tasks and revised 57 others, and Harvey LAB’s public set has grown from about 1,250 tasks to 2,010 since launching in May 2026. Like software, these releases can also introduce breaking changes—Terminal Bench can drop saturated tasks with each version, making scores hard to compare across releases. Deterministic checks over LLM judges. Code-based checks are reproducible and won’t shift rankings when a judge model is updated. DeepSWE and AutomationBench avoid LLM judges altogether, and Agents’ Last Exam goes to great lengths to minimize them. When an eval does need a judge—for a legal memo or clinical response—it narrows the judge’s job to binary yes/no rubric items rather than a holistic score. Graders check the outcome, not the steps. The intent is to allow any approach that produces the right result to pass. For example, Terminal Bench inspects the final state of the container and ignores the agent’s intermediate commands or console output. AutomationBench, OSWorld 2.0, and DeepSWE work the same way. All-pass scoring is common because partial work often isn’t usable. Under all-pass scoring, a task passes only if every test or criterion passes. DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, Terminal Bench Science, AutomationBench, and Harvey LAB score this way. As Harvey puts it, “there is no partial credit for catching most of the issues”—a report that flags eight of ten risks is incomplete, not 80% us

title: codex 0.172.0
summary:
New Features

  • Follow thread links from search results and transcripts to open saved conversations and nested agents in the terminal. (#62332)
  • Press Tab to complete arguments for supported slash commands. For example, /mcp lo completes to /mcp login. (#62343)
  • Jump between task groups in the agent command center with Shift+Up and Shift+Down. (#62200)
  • Optional stdio MCP servers with cached tool lists now start on their first tool call by default. (#62366)
  • Set an approval reviewer for individual connected app tools in config.toml. (#62360)
  • App-server clients can select Amazon Bedrock Runtime during setup or sign-in. (#62222)

Bug Fixes

  • codex exec resume restores saved sandbox permissions, the working directory, and workspace roots unless explicitly overridden. (#62194)
  • Remote sessions preserve working directories, workspace roots, and writable paths when the client and server run on different operating systems. (#62375, #62376, #62377)
  • Codex reports provider errors as soon as they arrive in a response stream and identifies which API spend limit was reached. (#62329, #62356)
  • Interrupting a parent turn preserves queued replies from child agents for the next turn. (#62348)
  • Use PageUp and PageDown to read and submit answer choices that are taller than the terminal’s answer area. (#62209)
  • Cloud replies that finish after history loads now update in place, keeping the terminal transcript in order. (#62403)

Documentation

  • The bundled openai-docs skill now covers migration to GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, including endpoint choices and tool-calling requirements. (#62447)

Chores

  • Code Mode now uses gRPC for all host connections. The code_mode_host_grpc setting is deprecated. (#62476)
  • Python formatting and SDK type generation now verify dependency hashes against the repository lockfile. (#62346)

content_excerpt: Make table and column context accessible for discovery, governance, and agentic workflows. We’re excited to announce support for catalog labels – a new capability in the Apache Iceberg™ REST Catalog API that enables platforms, engines, and agents to access context such as business purpose, ownership and data classifications maintained in Iceberg REST-compatible catalogs. This shared context supports discovery, governance, and agentic workflows across the data and AI ecosystem. We believe that catalog metadata should be as open and portable as the data it describes. As enterprises bring more tools into their open lakehouse architectures, they need a common way to share the context that makes their data understandable, useful, and secure for all teams, regardless of what tools they use. Today, that context often remains siloed in the source catalog. Data and AI teams must recreate classifications across platforms, maintain custom metadata synchronization pipelines, or work with agents that lack complete context. Databricks is joined by Google Cloud, Salesforce, ClickHouse, Atlan, Collibra, DataHub, Immuta, Trust3 AI, PhoenixAI, and Datastrato in advancing this shared vision of metadata interoperability. title: Transport-Safe Evaluation of LLM Agents: Trajectory-Dependent Judge Error and Anytime-Valid Auditing
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are often ranked by an LLM judge whose error rates are measured once and reused for every agent. The corrected success rates can then be biased when the judge's errors depend on the trajectory and agents differ in the trajectories they produce for successes or failures. We derive the exact asymptotic bias and give a chain of checks from identification to simultaneous ranks. On a four-agent semi-synthetic benchmark, a scalar correction with oracle calibration has maximum bias 0.245 and mean pointwise coverage 0.016, and never recovers the full ranking (0/250 replications). Augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) with a uniform or a design-aware random audit keeps the maximum bias below 0.003, with mean pointwise coverage of 0.939 and 0.950. In a 48-cell stress test, effective target support rises only from 0.209 to 0.805 as calibration grows from 600 to 4,800 labels, while audited AIPW keeps a mean absolute error of 0.018-0.020. Without calibration support, or with judge dependence within an externally justified bound, we report valid bounds or sensitivity sets and carry them into rank sets. An e-process confidence sequence stays valid, for a stable target, under predictable adaptive auditing and arbitrary stopping.

content_excerpt: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it. Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days. We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods. But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline. A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with. We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article). My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. title: Ultimate guide for fixing your team’s API keys
summary:
Most Gemini prototypes start the same way. You grab an API key from Google AI Studio, then paste it into your coding agent to start building a prototype. That speed is the point, and shouldn’t be slowed down. 

The trouble starts later, when the prototype gets real users and the key comes along unchanged. By then it usually isn't one key. Every developer has their own, often several, sitting in .env files, shell profiles and chat threads. The app has one more, baked into its config.

For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month. One of those keys ends up in a public repo, a Slack channel or a mobile app bundle. Automated scrapers find it within minutes and use it to run large workloads. By the time the first billing alert arrives, the bill is in the tens of thousands. Under the shared responsibility model, the customer pays for usage made with their own valid credentials. For a seed-stage company, that’s runway gone in a weekend.

In our recent post, 10 questions every startup should answer before moving to production with their AI prototype, we covered the whole path from prototype to production. This post goes deeper on one part of it: getting off raw API keys entirely.

Here is what this guide covers:

  • Authorize your people. Give everyone on the team one login with Application Default Credentials and use it to call Gemini, Claude and open models. Steps 1 and 2 take about five minutes.

  • Authorize your application. Run your app under its own service account with only the access it needs. Steps 3 and 4.

  • Lock down what's left. Move the remaining keys into Secret Manager, then add spend caps, guardrails and monitoring. Step 5 and the closing sections.

The code for every step is in a companion repo with runnable samples and offline tests.

Why a raw key is different

An AI Studio key is a bearer token. Whoever holds it can use it. It doesn't expire on its own. It isn't tied to a machine, a person or a workload. It has no spending limit unless you add one. When someone leaves the company, nobody knows which keys to revoke.

That is fine on your laptop while you are the only user. It stops being fine when any of these is true:

  • A key has left your laptop. It was shared in chat, committed to a repo or deployed to a server.

  • More than one person on the team needs to call the API.

  • You are spending more than a few hundred dollars a month, or you are about to onboard paying customers.

If one of those describes you, do the switch this week.

Before changing anything, find out where your keys are. The repo includes a small scanner that looks for strings shaped like Google API keys and for api_key= set to a literal value. It reports the file and line but never the key itself. It also exits with an error, so you can drop it into CI:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'python -m step1_keyless_auth.scan_for_keys .'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f774a2327d0>)])]>

Step one: Give each person one login

Each person on the team runs one command:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud auth application-default login'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f774a384d50>)])]>

A browser window opens, you sign in with your work account and gcloud stores a short-lived credential on your machine. Every Google Cloud SDK finds it automatically. There is no key to copy, paste or leak.

Then point your tools at the team project:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=my-startup-dev'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f774a387390>)])]>

Someone has to grant you access to the project first. Step four shows how.

Step two: Call any model with that login

That single credential works for every model in Model Garden, not only Gemini. You don't need new accounts, new keys or separate invoices. Within each SDK, switching models means changing one string.

Gemini, with the Google Gen AI SDK. If your prototype builds the client with api_key=..., this is the only change:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'from google import genai\r\n\r\nclient = genai.Client(enterprise=True, project="my-startup-dev", location="global")\r\nresp = client.models.generate_content(model="gemini-4-hydrogen", contents="Hi")\r\nprint(resp.text)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f774a386010>)])]>

enterprise=True sends the call to Gemini Platform instead of AI Studio. Older samples call the same flag vertexai=True, and current SDK versions accept both.

Claude, with Anthropic's SDK and the same login:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'from anthropic import AnthropicVertex\r\n\r\nclient = AnthropicVertex(project_id="my-startup-dev", region="global")\r\nmsg = client.messages.create(\r\n model="claude-sonnet-5-5",\r\n max_tokens=512,\r\n messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}],\r\n)\r\nprint(msg.content[0].text)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f774a386c90>)])]>

Open models such as OpenAI's gpt-oss, with the OpenAI SDK pointed at Google Cloud:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'import google.auth, google.auth.transport.requests\r\nfrom openai import OpenAI\r\n\r\ncreds, _ = google.auth.default(scopes=["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"])\r\ncreds.refresh(google.auth.transport.requests.Request())\r\n\r\nclient = OpenAI(\r\n base_url="https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/my-startup-dev/locations/global/endpoints/openapi",\r\n api_key=creds.token, # a one-hour token from your login, not a stored key\r\n)\r\nresp = client.chat.completions.create(\r\n model="openai/gpt-oss-120b-maas",\r\n messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}],\r\n)\r\nprint(resp.choices[0].message.content)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f774a387ad0>)])]>

Two things to know:

  • Partner models like Claude need a one-time Enable on their Model Garden card in each project. After that, everyone with access can call them.

  • OpenAI's GPT-6 models arrived in Model Garden on October 21 in private preview for select enterprise customers. When they open up, the same login will work for them too.

Every call lands on one Google Cloud bill, which makes it easier to compare models on cost and quality.

Step three: Give your app its own identity

Your app needs the same thing your developers just got: an identity instead of a key. For a workload, that identity is a service account.

The good news is that the code from Step 2 doesn't change. On your laptop, ADC picks up your own login. On Cloud Run, GKE or Compute Engine, it picks up a short-lived token for the service account attached to the workload, refreshed automatically. So there is nothing in your codebase to leak. A token that escapes is short-lived, usually about an hour, and it only carries the permissions of one service account.

Create the service account and deploy with it:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud iam service-accounts create agent-runtime \\\r\n --display-name="Runtime identity for the app"\r\n\r\ngcloud run deploy my-agent \\\r\n --image=us-docker.pkg.dev/my-startup-prod/agents/api:v1 \\\r\n --service-account=agent-runtime@my-startup-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com \\\r\n --region=us-central1'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f774a386390>)])]>

Keep people and production apart. Developers work in my-startup-dev under their own logins, and the app runs in my-startup-prod under its service account. A mistake in one doesn't spend the other's budget.

Step four: Give each identity only what it needs

Removing keys solves the leak problem. The next question is what each identity is allowed to do. If a person or a service account holds the Editor or Owner role, a stolen login or token can still delete resources, change permissions or read data it never needed.

Calling models takes one role, roles/aiplatform.user. The grant looks the same for both kinds of identity.

For people, grant it to a Google group, not to individuals. Onboarding and offboarding then become a group membership change:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-startup-dev \\\r\n --member="group:ai-builders@my-startup.com" \\\r\n --role="roles/aiplatform.user"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f774a387410>)])]>

For the app, grant it to the service account:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-startup-prod \\\r\n --member="serviceAccount:agent-runtime@my-startup-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \\\r\n --role="roles/aiplatform.user"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f774a386290>)])]>

It takes about 30 seconds longer than granting Editor. If anything is compromised later, the attacker gets one narrow role instead of the whole project. When someone leaves, remove them from the group and their access ends everywhere at once.

In the Cloud Console, the Grant access dialog has a Help me choose roles button. You describe the task in plain English and Gemini suggests predefined roles. By default the suggestions cover common tasks, which usually means a service's broad Admin, Editor or Viewer role. To get the narrow roles, say so:

What is the narrowest access a service account needs to call Gemini models on Agent Platform?

Three more controls are worth knowing:

  • If your project sits in an organization, the vertexai.allowedModels policy limits which models anyone can call. You list values such as publishers/google/models/gemini-4-hydrogen:predict, and everything else is blocked.

  • The repo includes a one-line audit that lists every service account holding Owner or Editor on a project. Run it now and again before each launch.

  • To stop new keys from being created, enforce Org Policies denying CREATE on apikeys.googleapis.com/Key for API keys and iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation for service account keys.

Step 5: Put the remaining keys in Secret Manager

Some keys won't go away, like Stripe, Slack or your email provider. They belong in Secret Manager, not in .env files, chat threads or the repo. Access works the way it did in Step 4: grant read access on each secret to the identity that needs it.

Test keys go to the developer group:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud secrets create stripe-test-key --data-file=-\r\ngcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding stripe-test-key \\\r\n --member="group:ai-builders@my-startup.com" \\\r\n --role="roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f774a387290>)])]>

Anyone in the group can then fetch the key with their own login:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=stripe-test-key'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f774a387e50>)])]>

Live keys stay in the production project, readable only by the app's service account. The app reads them at startup:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'from google.cloud import secretmanager\r\n\r\nsm = secretmanager.SecretManagerServiceClient()\r\nresp = sm.access_secret_version(\r\n name="projects/my-startup-prod/secrets/stripe-live-key/versions/latest"\r\n)\r\nstripe_key = resp.payload.data.decode("utf-8")'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f774a384810>)])]>

Reading --data-file=- from standard input keeps the value out of your shell history. Every read is tied to a named person or service account, and rotating a key means adding one new version. Nothing is redeployed and no file is copied between laptops.

Then finish the job. Go to the AI Studio API keys page and delete every key, personal or shared, that ever left a laptop. A key you have moved away from is still live until you delete it.

What the new setup gives you

Once your people and your app run on identities in a Google Cloud project, several protections become available that a bare key can't offer. You don't need all of them on day one. They are worth knowing about before your first launch.

A spend cap that pauses the service

Standard budget alerts send email while the bill keeps climbing. A spend cap budget, currently in Preview, does more. When estimated spend for one service in one project passes the amount you set, new requests to that service are paused until you lift the cap or the next month starts. Alerts go to billing admins and project owners at 50%, 80% and 100%.

You can create one in the console under Budgets & alerts by choosing Spend cap enforcement, or through the Budget API. The repo wraps the API call and has a dry-run flag so you can inspect the request first:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'python -m bonus_spend_cap.create_spend_cap \\\r\n --billing-account 012345-6789AB-CDEF01 --amount 500 --dry-run'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f774a385550>)])]>

Know the limits before relying on it. Each cap covers a single project and a single service. Agent Platform, the Gemini API, Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions are eligible today. Enforcement runs on estimated cost and is not instant. Any overage is billed as normal, so set the number below the amount you can actually afford to lose. A cap also pauses usage covered by commitments, and after you lift it the service can take up to an hour to recover.

Set one cap on the dev project and another on prod. An experiment then can't drain the budget your customers depend on. For a second layer, lower your Agent Platform quotas to what you really need, so a bug or an agent stuck in a loop runs into a ceiling instead of your card limit.

Guardrails on prompts and responses

As soon as real users can type into your app, someone will try to make it ignore its instructions. Model Armor screens prompts and responses for prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, malicious URLs and sensitive data. You create a template once, check each prompt against it and only call the model when it comes back clean. The repo has both halves.

A sandbox for model-written code

If your product lets the model write and run code, for example to analyze a customer's spreadsheet, that code should not run inside your application process. With code execution, the model runs Python in a Google-managed sandbox and hands back the result:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'config=types.GenerateContentConfig(\r\n tools=[types.Tool(code_execution=types.ToolCodeExecution())],\r\n)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f774a384550>)])]>

The generated code never sees your environment variables, your files or your database.

Someone watching for unusual behavior

Security Command Center surfaces threats and misconfigurations across the project, such as a service account suddenly calling an API it has never used or a workload contacting an unfamiliar host. Together with Cloud Audit Logs, which record who changed what and when, it also gives you the answers your first enterprise customer's security review will ask for. Because every call now comes from a named person or service account, those logs mean something.

Your 20-minute checklist

For your team:

  • Everyone runs gcloud auth application-default login.

  • Grant roles/aiplatform.user to one Google group, and enable the partner models you want.

  • Move shared test keys into Secret Manager, readable by the group.

For your app:

  • Deploy with a service account that holds roles/aiplatform.user and nothing broader.

  • Move live third-party keys into Secret Manager, readable only by that service account.

  • Set a spend cap on each project below the amount you can afford to lose.

For both: Run the key scanner, then delete every AI Studio key at aistudio.google.com/apikey.

None of this slows down building. You keep the speed of the prototype and every model in Model Garden stays one string away. Nobody on the team has to guard a key again. The full code, with a sample for every step and bonus above, is in the companion repo.
